title: A School Without Bells
passage:
When Seaside Junior High renovated its buildings, the principal proposed an unusual experiment: for one month, the school would stop using bells between most classes. Students would still have a visible schedule, and teachers would keep clocks in every room, but the familiar sound would disappear except for emergency signals. Supporters argued that students should learn to manage time rather than depend on a bell. Critics predicted chaos. Some teachers worried that classes would run late, while parents questioned whether younger students were ready for so much responsibility. During the first week, the critics seemed partly correct. Several classes ended late, and some students arrived after the next lesson had begun. Teachers also discovered that their classroom clocks were not perfectly synchronized. The school could have ended the experiment immediately, but the principal asked staff to identify which failures came from the idea itself and which came from poor preparation. The school synchronized clocks, placed large time displays in hallways, and asked teachers to give a two-minute warning before class ended. Students were encouraged to check the schedule during breaks instead of waiting for a sound. By the second week, late arrivals decreased. An unexpected change also appeared: corridors became calmer because hundreds of students no longer moved at exactly the same second. Some teachers allowed students to finish a final sentence before leaving, while others ended slightly early when an activity was complete. However, the experiment created new concerns. A student with attention difficulties said the bell had provided an important external reminder. Another student worried constantly about the time and checked the clock too often. In response, the school offered optional vibration timers and visual reminders. The debate then shifted. The question was no longer simply whether bells were good or bad, but how much structure different students needed. At the end of the month, the school surveyed students, teachers, and families. Most students preferred fewer bells, but many wanted a sound before lunch and at the end of the school day. Teachers were divided. Some valued the flexibility, while others felt that time management had become an extra task competing with instruction. The school adopted a mixed system: no bells between ordinary morning classes, but signals at several major transition points. Seaside's experiment did not prove that every school should remove bells. Its conditions mattered. The building was small enough that students could move quickly, clocks were visible, and staff spent time adjusting the system. A larger school might have different results. The principal emphasized this point in the final report. Educational experiments are sometimes discussed as if one successful example provides a universal answer, but local context changes what is practical. The real value of the experiment was not that it discovered the perfect bell schedule. It showed the school which functions the bells had been serving: coordination, reminders, reassurance, and control of movement. Once those functions were visible, the community could decide which ones should remain and which students could manage in other ways.

The school also examined whether removing bells changed how teachers used lesson time. Some teachers became better at planning endings because they could no longer rely on a sound to stop them. Others found themselves checking the clock too often, especially during discussion activities. The staff shared practical strategies, such as placing a small timer where only the teacher could see it or assigning a student timekeeper during group work. These adjustments showed that removing one external signal did not remove the need for coordination; it shifted that responsibility to other cues, habits, and people. The principal therefore warned against describing the experiment as a move from control to complete freedom. Students and teachers still needed structure, but they could decide which forms of structure were useful. That distinction helped the school improve the system instead of judging the idea by the first week of results.
translation:
シーサイド中学校が校舎改修をした際、校長は一か月間、授業間のチャイムをほとんど鳴らさない実験を提案しました。時間割と時計は残し、緊急時の信号だけは別にします。賛成派は、生徒がチャイムに頼らず時間管理を学ぶべきだと考え、反対派は授業の遅れや混乱を心配しました。最初の週は実際に授業が延びたり、次の授業に遅れる生徒が出たりし、教室ごとの時計がずれていることも判明しました。しかし校長は、失敗が考え方そのものによるのか、準備不足によるのかを分けて考えるよう求めました。時計を同期し、廊下に大きな表示を置き、教師が終了二分前に知らせるようにすると、遅刻は減りました。また全員が同時に動かないため廊下が落ち着くという予想外の利点もありました。一方、注意を保つのが難しい生徒にとってチャイムは重要な外部の合図であり、逆に時間を気にしすぎて何度も時計を見る生徒もいました。そこで振動タイマーや視覚的なリマインダーを選べるようにしました。議論は『チャイムが良いか悪いか』ではなく、『人によってどの程度の外部構造が必要か』へ変わりました。最終調査では生徒の多くがチャイム減少を好みましたが、昼食前や一日の終わりには合図が欲しいという声が多く、教師の意見は分かれました。学校は通常の午前授業間は鳴らさず、大きな切り替えの時だけ鳴らす混合方式を採用しました。この実験は全学校でチャイムをなくすべきだと証明したわけではありません。校舎の大きさ、時計の見やすさ、調整に使える時間など条件が違えば結果も変わります。重要だったのは完璧なチャイム制度を見つけたことではなく、チャイムが『時間の調整、注意喚起、安心感、人の移動をそろえること』という複数の機能を持っていたと明らかになったことでした。その機能が見えたことで、何を残し、何を別の方法に置き換えるか考えられるようになったのです。

学校は、チャイムをなくすことで教師の時間の使い方がどう変わるかも調べました。終了の音に頼れなくなったことで、授業の終わり方を上手に計画するようになった教師もいれば、話し合い活動中に時計を何度も確認するようになった教師もいました。そこで、教師だけが見える小さなタイマーや、グループ活動で生徒の時間係を置く方法などを共有しました。外部の合図を一つなくしても、時間調整そのものが不要になるわけではなく、その責任が別の合図、習慣、人へ移るだけだと分かりました。校長は、この実験を『管理から完全な自由へ』という単純な変化として捉えるべきではないと説明しました。必要な構造は残しながら、どんな形が役立つかを選べることが重要だったのです。
